title: Levack's The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe: Revised Statistical Estimates
description: Brian Levack published The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe in 1987, the first comprehensive English-language comparative survey of European witch prosecution, revising statistical estimates of total executions downward from the wildly inflated figures (nine million) circulated in popular and feminist literature to a scholarly estimate of approximately 40,000–60,000 deaths out of about 110,000 trials. Levack's systematic comparison across European regions showed that prosecution was geographically uneven, concentrated in the Holy Roman Empire, Scotland, and parts of France, while largely absent from England, Scandinavia, and Spain (in large-scale form). His analysis of the conditions promoting and inhibiting mass prosecution — centralized courts, appellate review, Roman law procedure — provided the analytical framework for subsequent comparative work.
historiographical_note: Levack's statistical estimates have been broadly accepted by subsequent scholarship, though debated in detail. Wolfgang Behringer, Jenny Gibbons, and others have contributed additional regional data that has slightly revised the totals. The reduction from millions to tens of thousands was historically significant: it made witch prosecution comparable to other periods of persecution rather than uniquely catastrophic, changing the political register of the historiography.
source_method: Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (1987; revised editions 1995, 2006); comparative regional scholarship
